candidate.answerReason: The children's age sum N years ago was T−3N, so T−N=2(T−3N). This gives T=5N and T/N=5.

methods.label: Express both age totals at the earlier time
methods.explanation:
The useful distinction is that Tom’s age decreases by \(N\) when we look back \(N\) years, while the sum of three children’s ages decreases by \(3N\). Since their current age sum is \(T\), their earlier age sum was \(T-3N\), and Tom’s earlier age was \(T-N\).

At that time his age was twice their total, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
T-N&=2(T-3N),\\
T-N&=2T-6N,\\
T&=5N.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(N\) years ago refers to a past time, \(N>0\). Dividing by \(N\) gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{T}{N}=5},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
methods.levelReason: A single linear age equation is sufficient; the children's individual ages are unnecessary.

candidate.annotationRationale: The main target is translating the earlier-age relationship into a linear equation. Writing the two age expressions and solving the equation with parentheses are supporting procedures.
